---
title: "Leaving out one unit at a time"
---

The [information-criteria page](information-criteria.qmd) approximated predictive discrepancy without constructing omitted-data predictions. [**Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV)**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html) instead makes one unit the test set at a time. The word *one* matters: here it means one Provo content-word position summary, conditional on all other positions, including positions from the same passage.

## Defining the rotation

Let the data contain $N$ position summaries. For each position $i$, fit the complete procedure to the data with $i$ removed. Write the fitted predictor as

$$
\widehat f_{-i}
$$

and its prediction as

$$
\widehat y_{-i}=\widehat f_{-i}(x_i).
$$

For a chosen loss $L$, the leave-one-out risk estimate is

$$
\widehat R_{\mathrm{LOO}}
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^N
L(y_i,\widehat y_{-i}).
$$

Each response is absent from its own fit. The fits still overlap extensively, so they are not independent replications of the study.

## Exact Bayesian LOO for the Provo models

We use the same [Provo position table and Gaussian mean models](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd#provo-corpus) as on the preceding pages. The Bayesian calculation fixes a normal-inverse-gamma prior before any position is omitted.

The source paper reports excluding fixations shorter than 80 ms and longer than 800 ms. Their log-scale midpoint sets the prior intercept mean; slope means are zero. The expected residual variance treats four standard deviations as spanning those study bounds, and each coefficient's conditional prior variance multiplier is derived from the same span. The inverse-gamma shape is a fixed computational setting, and its rate follows from the declared residual-variance mean.

This prior is calibrated to study-level measurement bounds, not to the observed Provo response values. It is a teaching prior, not a prior proposed by Luke and Christianson.

```{r}
#| label: provo-exact-loo
#| message: false
#| warning: false

provo <- utils::read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)

linear_fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits,
  data = provo
)
quadratic_fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits + I(cloze_surprisal_bits^2),
  data = provo
)
X_linear <- model.matrix(linear_fit)
X_quadratic <- model.matrix(quadratic_fit)
y <- provo$mean_log_ffd

make_prior <- function(X) {
  log_bounds <- log(c(80, 800))
  log_span <- diff(log_bounds)
  expected_sigma2 <- (log_span / 4)^2
  list(
    b0 = c(mean(log_bounds), rep(0, ncol(X) - 1L)),
    V0 = diag(rep(log_span^2 / expected_sigma2, ncol(X))),
    a0 = 3,
    d0 = 2 * expected_sigma2,
    lower_ms = min(exp(log_bounds)),
    upper_ms = max(exp(log_bounds))
  )
}

exact_nig_loo <- function(X, y, prior) {
  n <- nrow(X)
  V0_inverse <- solve(prior$V0)
  full_xtx <- crossprod(X)
  full_xty <- crossprod(X, y)
  full_yty <- sum(y^2)
  result <- data.frame(
    observation = seq_len(n),
    predictive_location = NA_real_,
    predictive_scale = NA_real_,
    predictive_df = NA_real_,
    log_predictive_density = NA_real_
  )

  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    xi <- matrix(X[i, ], nrow = 1L)
    yi <- y[i]
    Vn <- solve(V0_inverse + full_xtx - crossprod(xi))
    bn <- drop(Vn %*% (
      V0_inverse %*% prior$b0 + full_xty - drop(xi) * yi
    ))
    an <- prior$a0 + (n - 1L) / 2
    dn <- as.numeric(
      prior$d0 + 0.5 * (
        full_yty - yi^2 +
          t(prior$b0) %*% V0_inverse %*% prior$b0 -
          t(bn) %*% solve(Vn) %*% bn
      )
    )
    location <- drop(xi %*% bn)
    scale <- sqrt(
      (dn / an) * (1 + drop(xi %*% Vn %*% t(xi)))
    )
    degrees <- 2 * an

    result$predictive_location[i] <- location
    result$predictive_scale[i] <- scale
    result$predictive_df[i] <- degrees
    result$log_predictive_density[i] <-
      dt((yi - location) / scale, df = degrees, log = TRUE) -
      log(scale)
  }
  result
}

linear_prior <- make_prior(X_linear)
quadratic_prior <- make_prior(X_quadratic)
linear_loo <- exact_nig_loo(X_linear, y, linear_prior)
quadratic_loo <- exact_nig_loo(X_quadratic, y, quadratic_prior)

loo_summary <- data.frame(
  model = c("Linear", "Quadratic"),
  omitted_positions = nrow(provo),
  exact_elpd_loo = c(
    sum(linear_loo$log_predictive_density),
    sum(quadratic_loo$log_predictive_density)
  ),
  exact_loo_rmse = c(
    sqrt(mean((y - linear_loo$predictive_location)^2)),
    sqrt(mean((y - quadratic_loo$predictive_location)^2))
  )
)
loo_summary

loo_plot <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = provo$cloze_surprisal_bits,
  observed = y,
  linear = linear_loo$predictive_location,
  quadratic = quadratic_loo$predictive_location
)
loo_plot <- loo_plot[order(loo_plot$cloze_surprisal_bits), ]

ggplot2::ggplot(
  loo_plot,
  ggplot2::aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, observed)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.18, color = "grey25") + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    ggplot2::aes(y = linear, linetype = "Linear"),
    linewidth = 0.65,
    color = "grey25"
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    ggplot2::aes(y = quadratic, linetype = "Quadratic"),
    linewidth = 0.65,
    color = "#2B6CB0"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Linear" = 2, "Quadratic" = 1)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Observed and LOO-predicted mean log FFD",
    linetype = "LOO mean"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

Conjugacy gives a Student-$t$ predictive density for every omitted position. Exact ELPD is `r sprintf("%.3f", loo_summary$exact_elpd_loo[loo_summary$model == "Linear"])` for the linear model and `r sprintf("%.3f", loo_summary$exact_elpd_loo[loo_summary$model == "Quadratic"])` for the quadratic model. The corresponding RMSEs are `r sprintf("%.5f", loo_summary$exact_loo_rmse[loo_summary$model == "Linear"])` and `r sprintf("%.5f", loo_summary$exact_loo_rmse[loo_summary$model == "Quadratic"])` on the mean log-duration scale.

The raw points and LOO predictive means remain on the same axes. This matters because a small aggregate advantage can otherwise hide where the two fitted functions differ.

## What one means here

One omitted unit is a content-word position summary. Other positions from the same passage remain in the training data, and the response already averages over readers. The target is thus one position summary conditional on the remaining position table. It is not a new passage, reader, participant response, or word type.

The distinction persists even though every position receives an out-of-sample prediction. Summing pointwise scores within a passage would not retroactively remove that passage from fitting. A passage target requires leave-one-passage-out validation from the start.

## Computation, tuning, and overlap

Literal LOO usually requires $N$ fits, which can be expensive. Conjugacy makes all `r nrow(provo)` Provo calculations available analytically. The next page evaluates whether posterior draws from the full fit can approximate these exact omitted-position quantities.

Any response-adaptive tuning would still have to occur within each (N-1) training set. Fixing a transformation or penalty after consulting all responses would let the omitted response influence its own prediction.

The training sets also overlap. Two LOO fits share all but their two distinct omitted positions. This dependence does not invalidate the mean score, but it rules out treating the position fits as independent study replications.

## Checking the omitted unit

1. What empirical object does one Provo LOO unit represent?
2. Which data remain available when a position is omitted?
3. Why is this not an omitted-passage analysis?
4. Which part of the prior uses the source-study measurement bounds?

LOO-CV gives every position a prediction from a fit that excluded it. The [previous page](information-criteria.qmd) used an in-sample approximation; the [next page](psis-loo.qmd) approximates these exact Bayesian omitted-position densities using full-posterior draws.
